title: Perfect or Nothing
objective: After this level you can spot the perfect-solution fallacy: rejecting an idea because it doesn't solve the whole problem.
summary: The perfect-solution fallacy rejects a real improvement because it isn't total. Seat belts cut deaths by about half. Demsetz's fix: compare real options, not reality with an ideal.

cards.headline: "Seat belts don't save everyone. So why bother wearing one?"
cards.body: Said out loud, it sounds silly. Yet the same shape of argument turns up everywhere: a spelling checker is useless because it misses some typos; a new bike lane is pointless because some cyclists will still ride in traffic. This level names the pattern and gives you one question that deflates it.

cards.fact: Seat belts cut serious crash injuries and deaths by about half.
cards.context: That's the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's figure. About half is not all, so some people wearing belts still die in crashes. "Not all" is exactly the gap the hook's argument pounces on, as if a huge improvement counted for nothing because it isn't total.

cards.headline: The perfect-solution fallacy
cards.body: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls it the perfectionist fallacy: rejecting a proposal solely because it doesn't solve the problem perfectly, in cases where perfection isn't really required. It also goes by the perfect solution fallacy or the nirvana fallacy. The hidden rule is "if it isn't perfect, it isn't worth doing". Notice the fine print, though: sometimes perfection really is required. A lock that works most days isn't much of a lock.

cards.headline: Compared with what?
cards.body: In 1969 the economist Harold Demsetz criticized what he called the nirvana viewpoint: find gaps between the ideal and the real, then conclude the real is failing. He urged comparing real alternatives instead, and economists now call the mistake the Nirvana fallacy. That gives you the question that deflates it: compared with what? Not belts against a crash nobody gets hurt in. Belts against no belts.

cards.headline: Perfect-or-nothing: spotted
learned: Rejecting a fix for not being total is a fallacy
Seat belts cut deaths by about half

questions.prompt: Match each one with what the cards say about perfection and its alternatives.

pairs.left: A lock that works most days

questions.explanation: Seat belts cut serious crash injuries and deaths by about half. Harold Demsetz criticized the nirvana viewpoint. And a lock that works most days isn't much of a lock, since there perfection really is required.

questions.prompt: Why does "seat belts don't save everyone" fail as a reason not to wear one?

options.label: It compares belts with perfection, not with no belts
Seat belts actually do save everyone who wears them
options.rationale: They cut deaths by about half, not all.

options.label: Nobody has measured what belts do
The argument is too short to judge
options.rationale: Length isn't the flaw; the comparison is.

questions.explanation: The fair comparison is belts against no belts, and belts cut serious injuries and deaths by about half.

questions.prompt: A school rejects a crossing guard because some kids will still cross badly. What question exposes the flaw?

options.label: "Who first suggested a crossing guard?"
options.rationale: Who suggested it doesn't affect whether it helps.

options.label: "Compared with no guard at all, is it better?"
"Is a crossing guard natural?"
options.rationale: That's Level 54's trap, and beside the point here.

questions.explanation: Demsetz's question: compare the real option with the real alternative, not with a perfect world.
